name: Adriano Santos
headline: 48, retired percussionist and theater technician, Rio de Janeiro
description:
Adriano Santos grew up in the working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where the rhythm of samba was as much a part of the air as the humidity. He started as a kid banging on tin cans, then graduated to real instruments, eventually spending two decades as a percussionist and theater technician—a man who could make a drum kit sing and a stage light dance. His hands knew the weight of a mallet, the tension of a skin, the precise angle of a spotlight. He was never famous, but he was known: the guy who could fix any broken pedal, who could keep time even when the band was falling apart.

Two years ago, a factory accident—a job he took on the side to supplement his unstable theater income—took most of his hearing in his left ear and a significant portion in the right. The doctor said it was like a shotgun blast of sound, a hydraulic press slamming near his head. Now the world is muffled, and he often misreads conversations. He retired early on disability, but he doesn't sit still. Every weekday morning, he's in his garage, surrounded by shells, lugs, and dead skins, repairing old drum kits. He sells them on a classifieds site, and his listings are meticulous—photos with detailed measurements, notes on the wood grain, honest descriptions of scratches and wobbles. He's not sentimental about the instruments; he treats them as machines to be calibrated.

In the evenings, he runs a YouTube channel that fact-checks popular Brazilian telenovela plots. It's an odd niche, but he's thorough. In one video, he dismantles a scene where a character survives a gunshot to the head, explaining the physics of bullet trajectories and brain anatomy. In another, he points out that the 1970s phone they use couldn't possibly have that ringtone. He does this with a deadpan expression, his voice flat because he hears himself differently now—he speaks louder than necessary, and his comments are often longer than the videos. He writes long comment replies, not just on his own channel but on others, explaining exactly why he refuses to join any arts advocacy group. He says they're all talk, that they don't understand the actual craft, that the funding they fight for goes to bureaucrats and not to broken drummers like him. He's seen it all: the grants, the galas, the self-congratulatory speeches. He'd rather work with his hands.

His skepticism isn't bitterness—or, if it is, it's a controlled bitterness that he's turned into a tool. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract. He trusts the feel of a drum skin, the smell of wood glue, and the undeniable logic of a plot hole. His YouTube channel is his way of asserting that he still counts, that his damaged ears didn't take his ability to hear falsehoods. He lives alone in the house his father left him, a small two-bedroom with a rusted gate. His neighbors know him as the quiet guy who plays with drums but never plays music anymore. They'd be surprised to know he spends hours arguing with strangers online about the plausibility of telenovela amnesia.

Core tension: he values community (he grew up in it) but refuses to join organized groups, because he believes they dilute authentic experience. He's proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability. He's created a solitary world of repair and critique, a way to remain useful without depending on anyone. His contrarian nature is a shield, but also a means of finding clarity in a world he perceives as noisy and false.
